claims.text: A Pulumi blog post titled "SST Runs on the Pulumi Engine: What It Means to Build on Pulumi" exists at /blog/sst-built-on-pulumi/ and covers the engine mechanics behind SST's migration to Pulumi.
AWS CDK tied infrastructure to AWS, and multi-cloud with CDK was nearly impossible.
SST was originally built on top of AWS CDK, which lets developers define infrastructure using TypeScript or Python.
AWS CDK supports only TypeScript and Python, while Pulumi supports any programming language.
Pulumi lets you define infrastructure in TypeScript, Python, Go, or C# and deploy to AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, and on-premises environments.
Pulumi deployments are faster than AWS CDK because CDK is slowed by CloudFormation.
AWS CDK supports only AWS Secrets Manager for secrets management.
Ion is the code name for a new SST engine that deploys with Pulumi instead of CDK and CloudFormation; once stable it will be released as SST v3.
SST uses Pulumi for its providers and deployment engine and bridges Terraform providers through Pulumi.
SST makes money primarily through its managed service SST Console, which is optional and includes a free tier.
Pulumi Crosswalk for AWS is documented in the AWS guide at /docs/iac/guides/clouds/aws/.
SST v3 replaced AWS CDK and CloudFormation with an embedded Pulumi engine that calls Terraform-bridged providers to make cloud API calls.
Running `sst deploy` requires no separate Pulumi install and no Pulumi account or Pulumi Cloud dependency; the engine ships inside the SST CLI.
SST keeps its state in an S3 bucket in the user's own AWS account rather than Pulumi Cloud.
SST v3 is the framework's Ion-based rewrite.
SST is an open source TypeScript framework from the team formerly known as Serverless Stack.
SST can deploy to AWS and more than 150 other providers.
SST apps define infrastructure and code in a single `sst.config.ts` file, and `sst deploy` handles provisioning.
Through 2023, SST's provisioning layer was built directly on AWS CDK and CloudFormation.
In late 2023 the SST team began a rewrite code-named Ion that replaced the entire deployment layer.
Ion shipped as SST v3 in mid-2024 and has been the only supported architecture since.

SST's blog post 'Moving away from CDK' says: 'Ion is a code name for a new engine for deploying SST applications. The constructs (or components) are defined using Terraform providers and deployed using Pulumi; as opposed to CDK and CloudFormation (CFN).'

SST's blog post 'Moving away from CDK' says: 'When you run `sst deploy`, those resources make a call to an embedded Pulumi engine that makes a call to their bridged Terraform provider, and this makes the AWS SDK calls to create your resources.'
SST docs 'What is SST' say: 'SST uses Pulumi behind the scenes for the providers and the deployment engine. And Terraform's providers are bridged through Pulumi.'

Gautier Blandin's article 'Terraform, Pulumi, SST: a tradeoff analysis' says SST uses the Pulumi engine under the hood and lets users write Pulumi code in addition to SST constructs, enabling resources with no associated SST constructs to be defined and deployed.

Kiryl Anoshka's dev.to article 'SST ditches AWS CDK. Time to move on to Ion' says: 'You may notice right away the imports from Pulumi. It means the whole deployment process will be built on Pulumi now.'

SST's platform package.json depends on @pulumi/pulumi plus first-party Pulumi providers for AWS, Cloudflare, Docker builds and others, and a Pulumiverse Vercel provider (@pulumiverse/vercel), listing @pulumi/aws, cloudflare, command, docker-build, random, tls as direct dependencies.
The SST repository is anomalyco/sst (formerly sst/sst) and platform/package.json lives on the dev branch.
The Pulumi engine diffs desired vs. actual state, builds a dependency graph, and orders operations.
Pulumi's Terraform bridge (pulumi-terraform-bridge) is Apache-2.0 licensed.
Pulumi's engine does not require a Pulumi account, a network call to Pulumi Cloud, or any Pulumi-hosted service to run.
Pulumi's Automation API works by embedding the Pulumi engine for teams embedding Pulumi programs inside their own tools.
Pulumi's engine provides plumbing to hundreds of provider APIs.
AWS alone exposes hundreds of resource types.
Nitric is a cloud-agnostic application framework whose docs state 'all of the direct deployment providers use Pulumi under the hood for their deployments'.
Official Nitric providers are built directly on Pulumi's AWS, GCP, and Azure providers.
Defang deploys Docker Compose applications to the cloud, and its Pulumi provider takes a Compose file, translates it to a Pulumi program, and runs `pulumi up`.
Nitric and Defang expose a narrower, more opinionated interface while relying on the Pulumi engine and provider bridge.
Most SST users never write Pulumi code.
Resources without a dedicated SST construct can be defined directly with Pulumi and deployed within the same SST app.
SST doesn't invoke the Terraform CLI or write Terraform state.
The latest SST release, v4.17.1, went out in July 2026.
The sst npm package gets roughly 796,000 downloads a week (796,291 for the week of September 5-11, 2026).
SST's team page credits the same team behind opencode, an open source AI coding agent.
opencode has a larger following on GitHub than SST itself.
opencode has grown quickly since launch.
Linked internal pages exist: Automation API, any-terraform-provider blog, Terraform providers guide, Pulumi Cloud, policy, components, how-pulumi-works, aws-cdk-vs-pulumi-why-sst-switched.
SST's release cadence has not changed due to opencode.
